blocks.46175673: Two open protocols connect the parts. The Model Context Protocol (MCP, Anthropic, 2024) gives a standard method for an application to give tools and data to a model. For example, an MCP server makes a calendar or a database available, and each agent that uses MCP can use it. Agent2Agent (A2A, Google, 2025) lets agents from different vendors give tasks to each other. Both are now open projects of the Linux Foundation.

blocks.64150453: Week 5 introduced pretrained and adapted language models. A model that learned to predict text does not automatically try to be helpful or follow the intent of a user. Human feedback can give another training signal. People compare outputs, a model learns to predict these preferences, and then we can optimize a policy with this learned reward. This is one family of methods, usually with the name RL from human feedback (RLHF).
blocks.69534063: Because the robot has a physical body, there are some gaps. The reality gap is between simulation and physical deployment. The semantic gap is between sensor values and objects and situations that have a meaning. The control gap is between a planned motion and what the hardware, which is not perfect, really does. A robust robot does these steps again and again: it estimates, it acts, it measures the result and it corrects. Thus, autonomy usually has layers. Low-level controllers keep the motion stable. Planners select actions. People give goals, supervise exceptions or share the control.
blocks.84746386: Orchestrator–workers: one model divides the task at run time. It gives the parts to workers and combines their results.

blocks.de6243e6: Week 5 examined how neural models represent context, generate content and adapt to tasks. A capable model is not yet a complete agent. Someone must decide what the model can do, how it interprets observations, how it selects actions and when it must stop. This week studies this larger system. Our example for the full week is a delivery robot on a campus. We compare it with agents that play games and with language models that use tools.
blocks.c93ed860: These questions are connected. But they are not a recipe that each agent must implement completely. A rule-based controller possibly does not learn. A planner can use a known model. An LLM agent can use tools without online RL. The core learning goal is this: explain these differences, and solve a small sequential decision problem step by step. The linked research papers and the advanced families of algorithms give optional depth. The ethics material later in the course examines the wider questions of goals, responsibility and human authority.
blocks.7afffc79: An agent is a system that perceives an environment and does actions in it. This definition includes a thermostat, a chess program, a delivery robot and an LLM that selects tools. The important change is this: the system does not only predict an answer. It selects an action, and the results of the action change what occurs next. Thus, an agent works in a loop: it observes, it updates an internal state, it selects an action and it observes the result.
blocks.b4357eb2: A rational agent selects the action that it expects to give the best result, as its performance measure defines it. It uses what it perceived and what it knows. Rational does not mean that the agent knows everything or that it is morally good. A route planner can be rational when it selects a road that is blocked later: it used the information that it had. Rationality also does not mean unlimited computation. Real agents have deadlines, finite memory, models that are not complete and limited energy. Bounded rationality asks which good actions are possible within these limits.
blocks.a9b6286e: Thus, the performance measure is an important design decision, not only an administrative task. If a delivery system gets a reward only for speed, it can drive dangerously. If a chatbot gets a reward for engagement, it can make an unhelpful conversation longer. Proxy measures are useful, because goals such as “help the user” are difficult to calculate. But when you optimize a proxy, the system can show behaviour that you did not intend. This is the start of the alignment problem: how can the behaviour that comes from an objective stay consistent with human intentions and limits?
blocks.6017489c: Before you select an algorithm for an agent, specify the task. A useful checklist is PEAS: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators and Sensors. An example is an autonomous delivery robot on a campus. Its performance measure can combine successful deliveries, travel time, energy use, comfort of pedestrians near it and prevention of collisions. Its environment includes paths, doors, lifts, people, weather and other vehicles. Its actuators include wheels, brakes, a lock on the compartment, lights and possibly speech. Its sensors can include cameras, lidar, wheel encoders, GPS, inertial sensors and signals from the delivery compartment.
blocks.756247a3: PEAS shows assumptions that are otherwise easy to hide. “Deliver quickly” is not a sufficient objective. How do we count failed deliveries? How much delay is acceptable near pedestrians? Who can open the compartment? In the same way, a research assistant that uses tools needs more than a language model. Its environment includes documents, databases, websites, user instructions and the policies of the institution. Its actuators can include search, creation of files, execution of code and messages. Its sensors include prompts, tool outputs, permissions and error messages.
blocks.1688874b: Task environments are different in some dimensions, and these dimensions have a large effect on the architecture. An environment is fully observable when the agent can get all of the state that is relevant for its decision. It is partially observable when the observations are not complete or have noise. It is deterministic when an action and a state set the next state. It is stochastic when more than one outcome is possible. In an episodic task, one decision has no effect on later cases. In a sequential task, the current action changes the choices in the future. Environments can also be static or dynamic, discrete or continuous, known or unknown at the start, and single-agent or multi-agent.
blocks.089af899: Chess is fully observable and discrete, but it is adversarial and sequential. Driving is partially observable, stochastic, continuous, dynamic and multi-agent. People often treat document classification as episodic and static. An LLM agent that works on a live software repository is sequential and partially observable: a file can change between two observations, tools can fail, and another developer can change the same code. When we know these properties, we do not use a solution for a clean puzzle in a real environment that changes.
blocks.83a10fc3: A language model changes a context into probable tokens. An agentic system puts such a model in a loop with memory, tools, an action policy, observations and stop conditions. The model can propose an action. The system around it validates the action and executes it. A call to an API is not intelligent by itself. It increases what the system can change. Thus, the system needs more permissions control, monitoring and recovery.
blocks.40e5732b: Reading: Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 4th ed., Chapter 2. This chapter explains the agent framework, PEAS and the classification of environments that we use here.
blocks.6b65dd20: A simple reflex agent uses condition–action rules: if the temperature is low, turn on the heating. It is fast, but it fails when the current observation does not show everything that is relevant. A model-based agent keeps an internal state, for example an estimate of where a robot is. It updates this state when new observations come. A goal-based agent evaluates actions by whether they reach a wanted state. It often uses search or planning. A utility-based agent compares trade-offs between outcomes, for example speed, safety, energy and comfort. A learning agent changes its behaviour from data or experience. Real systems usually combine these ideas. They do not fit in only one class.
blocks.0f97c576: In which state am I probably?
blocks.ab5a5092: How must behaviour change with experience?
blocks.c25121cd: Needs correct feedback and safe exploration
blocks.1ae243ad: Modern LLM agents often use a repeated plan–act–observe cycle. The model gets a goal and the current context. It proposes a tool call. It gets the result of the tool. It continues until it gives an answer or until a stop rule applies. Useful components are a tool registry, working memory, longer-term retrieval, a planner and an evaluator. Reliability comes from good engineering of the full loop: typed tool interfaces, least-privilege permissions, limits on time and cost, validation of outputs, logging, and human approval for important actions.
blocks.d9dfe1d6: An LLM has a finite context window. It does not have a permanent memory of its own history. Thus, agent systems use different types of memory. Working memory keeps the current goal, intermediate results and recent observations. Episodic memory keeps previous trajectories or results of tasks. Semantic memory finds facts and documents, often with embeddings. Procedural memory is in instructions, tools, code or learned policies. More memory is not always better. Retrieved information that is not relevant can distract the model. Old information can disagree with the current environment. Stored material can contain sensitive data.
blocks.2b571d3b: Planning also has different forms. A model can make a full plan before it acts. It can change between one reasoning step and one tool call (the ReAct pattern of Yao et al., 2023). It can make several possible plans and compare them. Or it can use a separate evaluator, which decides if the progress is sufficient. A long plan can become old after the first unexpected observation. But an agent that only reacts can lose the global goal. Effective systems often combine a rough plan with frequent new planning.
blocks.98042fd3: A tool changes a generated symbol into an action outside the model. Thus, the interface of a tool must specify the necessary arguments, the valid types, the possible errors, the side effects and the permissions. To read a calendar and to delete an event must not have the same authority. A robust execution layer validates the arguments. It asks for confirmation when it is difficult to reverse the results. It records what occurred, and it gives back structured observations. The model can write fluently, but the tool layer decides what the system can really change.
blocks.4480cdac: When an agent fails, the cause is often the loop, not only the language generation. The model can select the wrong tool, or use a correct tool with incorrect arguments. It can read a result incorrectly, or repeat an action without end. It can stop before it verifies the success, or continue after it reached the goal. Retrieved documents or web pages can also contain instructions that disagree with the goal of the user. This is a type of prompt injection. The observation is text. Thus, the model possibly cannot see the difference between trusted system instructions and content that is not trusted, unless the architecture makes this difference clear.

blocks.7ddf8a60: Research example: Yao et al. (2023), ReAct, studies language-model systems that change between reasoning steps and actions. It shows an architecture. It does not make sure that the reasoning is reliable or that the execution is safe.
blocks.b1333740: The agent architectures above explain how a system can select and execute actions. But they do not explain how it learns which actions to select. A controller that a person wrote, or a planner that gets a model, can act without reinforcement learning. We introduce RL when we want to make the behaviour better from the results of interaction. Then we do not have to give the correct action for each situation.
blocks.82b4af32: Look at our delivery robot on the campus. At a junction, it can take a short route with many people or a longer quiet route. Possibly it must also charge its battery before it accepts another delivery. Usually, no labelled example tells which action is best at each moment. Also, the action of the robot changes the situations that it will find later. Thus, the problem is different from the classification of a fixed image. When the robot selects an action, it also changes its future data and opportunities.
blocks.64b8c41f: Because results can come late, credit assignment is important (to find which action caused a result). When the battery of a robot becomes empty, the important mistake was possibly some actions before, when the robot went past a charger. A chess move can change a game where the reward comes only at the end. The learning problem is to connect actions with the results that come after them. It is not sufficient to reward only the last action before a success.
blocks.569d4952: Before we select a learning algorithm, we need a precise description of the decision problem. Which information defines a situation? Which actions are possible? What changes after an action, and which result is good? A Markov decision process (MDP) puts these questions into one model. It is a framework to state a problem. It is not a learning algorithm, and it is not a type of neural network.
blocks.2f77d99d: A usual discounted formulation describes the task with (S, A, P, R, \gamma). It also has a distribution of start states and the rules for the end of an episode. Rewards can be random (stochastic). More generally, the model gives a joint distribution of the next state and the reward. When we write down these elements, the robot does not have to know their probabilities already. The elements describe what the environment does. An algorithm can have access to this model, estimate it, or learn without an explicit representation of it.
blocks.9cc9b05f: The Markov assumption is about the distributions of the next state and of the reward. When we know the current state and action, these distributions do not need the full history. Thus, the definition of the state is important. The location alone is not sufficient if the result of a move also depends on the remaining battery charge. When we add the battery charge to the state, the representation gives more information. Thus, “Markov” does not mean that the past is not important. It means that the state contains a summary of the past information that this prediction needs.
blocks.2a37c395: The state is not the same as the observation. A camera image can hide a pedestrian behind a door. It possibly does not show how slippery a path is. For these cases, we use a partially observable model, frequently a POMDP. The agent can act with its history of observations, with a learned memory or with a belief state: a distribution over the possible true states. This connects to the material about probabilistic reasoning from earlier weeks. For the first numerical example, we assume on purpose a small state space that the agent can observe.
blocks.9dc3bcd3: Reading: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, Chapter 3, gives the MDP formulation. Russell & Norvig, Chapters 16–17, connect utility and sequential decisions. An MDP is suitable for one decision-maker. You can use it for chess against an opponent with a fixed policy. But when the players adapt to each other (strategic interaction), you need game-theoretic or multi-agent models.
blocks.8c4ef441: When the task is specified, we can state what the agent must learn. A policy specifies how the agent selects actions. In a fully observed MDP, we frequently write it as \pi(a \mid s). A deterministic policy selects one action for a state. A stochastic policy gives probabilities. The policy is the rule for the behaviour. It is different from the transition model, which describes how the environment responds.
blocks.c6d306eb: The objective is the expected return, not only the next reward. For a discounted episode, the return from the time t is
blocks.a755fb81: until the episode ends. With \gamma = 0, only the next reward is important. Values nearer to 1 give more weight to later results. Some finite episodic formulations use \gamma = 1. Discounting is a modelling decision. It does not replace safety constraints.
blocks.346cdd92: Worked comparison: a short route gives the rewards −1 and then +10. A longer route gives −1, −1 and then +10. With \gamma = 0.9, their returns from the start are -1 + 0.9 \times 10 = 8 and -1 - 0.9 + 0.9^2 \times 10 = 6.2. With these assumptions, the first route is better. If the first route has a large probability of an expensive failure, the comparison must include this uncertainty. The return makes the comparison explicit. But it does not tell which reward design is ethically acceptable.
blocks.04bb47ec: Check your understanding: charging costs time now. Why can it be rational for the robot to charge? Because the charge makes later rewards possible that the robot cannot get with its current battery charge. You must think about the state, the transition dynamics and the return together.
blocks.7d84b201: If the agent knows the transitions and the rewards, it can plan: it calculates the results of the possible actions. Dynamic programming is one family of methods that solve known finite MDPs. If the model is not known, the agent must learn from experience. Model-based RL estimates a model and uses it to plan. Model-free RL learns values or a policy. It does not first build an explicit transition model.
blocks.a6c88553: This distinction prevents a usual confusion: when we use an MDP, we do not have to use model-based RL. Q-learning can work in an MDP, and it learns directly from sampled transitions. Also, a system can solve a given MDP with planning, without learning from new interaction. Thus, the search methods from earlier weeks and RL are related tools. They are not two names for the same thing.
blocks.86c6decc: It is expensive to compare all possible future routes from the start. A value function gives a summary: the expected return from a state when the agent follows a policy. The action-value function Q_\pi(s, a) gives the return that we expect if the agent takes the action a in the state s and then follows \pi. The optimal action-value function Q^*(s, a) assumes that the agent continues optimally. Always know which policy you evaluate. A good state can have a low value if the policy after it is bad.
blocks.a00122c7: The Bellman principle divides the long-term value into two parts: the immediate reward and the discounted value of what comes after. For example, for a policy,
blocks.0783abfb: The expectation includes the action that \pi selects and the uncertain transition. This recursive relation is useful, because it connects decisions that are next to each other. We do not have to look at each full trajectory as a separate object.
blocks.006b8f34: Now we introduce Q-learning, because it changes this relation into a simple update from experience. It is a concrete example: the agent learns to compare actions when it does not have the full transition model. This gives the reason for the method before we show its formula.
blocks.58db00c5: For a small discrete task, keep one estimate for each state–action pair in a Q-table. After the agent takes the action a in the state s, it observes the reward r and the next state s'. Calculate the target r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'), and move the old estimate toward it:
blocks.f187afd7: The term in brackets is the temporal-difference (TD) error. The learning rate \alpha controls the size of the update. \gamma controls the weight of later rewards. They have different functions. At a true terminal state, the value of what comes after is zero. When an episode stops because of a time limit, this is not always a terminal event. Thus, an implementation must make a distinction between the two cases.
blocks.dbc369f8: In a state next to the goal, a move to the right gives the reward 10, and the episode ends. If the old Q-value is 2 and \alpha = 0.5, the target is 10, and the new estimate is 2 + 0.5\,(10 - 2) = 6. Now look at the state before it. There, a move to the right gives the reward 0 and goes to the state whose best estimate is 6. With \gamma = 0.9, the target is 5.4. If the old estimate is 1, the update gives 1 + 0.5\,(5.4 - 1) = 3.2.
blocks.d180de8b: This is how information about a later goal can change the estimate for an earlier action. The intermediate estimate 6 is not the true terminal reward. It is the current estimate after one update, and more experience can change it. The convergence guarantees for tabular Q-learning need assumptions, for example sufficient exploration and suitable learning rates. They are not automatically true for all neural-network approximations.
blocks.793733bc: The agent starts at the bottom left. The goal gives +10 and the pit gives −10. Both end the episode. All other moves give 0. Each move updates one Q-value with the rule above. The learning rate starts at 0.5 and the discount at 0.9, as in the worked example. With the probability ε, the agent selects a random action. Otherwise it selects the best known action. Look at how the information about the goal moves back, one transition at a time.
blocks.73f35a47: Primary reference: Watkins & Dayan (1992), Q-learning. For a textbook explanation with examples, see Sutton & Barto, Chapter 6.
blocks.c8b87030: The robot cannot learn which route is better if it always takes the route that looks best at the start. Exploitation uses the current knowledge. Exploration collects information that can make future decisions better. An \varepsilon-greedy behaviour rule usually selects an action that is best now. But with the probability \varepsilon, it selects a random action to explore. Exploration is a property of the data collection. It is not an extra reward label.
blocks.c59710ec: Random exploration is acceptable in a small simulator. But near people or expensive equipment, it can be dangerous. Then you can need constrained actions, simulation, demonstrations and human oversight. Also examine the reward. If the reward is for the distance that the robot travels, not for successful deliveries, the robot can learn to move without a purpose. A reward with a precise specification can still contain the wrong goal. For concrete problems with reward design and safe exploration, see Amodei et al. (2016).
blocks.fbfb18c5: Q-learning is a starting point. It is not the only method to learn actions. The next table puts the methods into groups, by what they represent and update. These groups overlap. For example, an actor–critic method can use a learned model, and a value-based method can use a neural network.
blocks.89a1483c: On-policy and off-policy is a different distinction. On-policy methods learn about the policy that makes their data. Off-policy methods can learn about a different target policy. The update of Q-learning uses a greedy continuation, also when an exploratory action made the transition. Thus, the agent can use past experience again. But this does not make all logged datasets sufficient for reliable learning.
blocks.06f4a756: Deep RL uses a neural network to approximate a value function, a policy or a model, when a table is not practical. The ideas of representation learning from Weeks 4–5 now support actions, not only classification or generation. Training is still difficult. Observations that follow each other are correlated. The estimated targets change during learning. One parameter update can change many states. Replay buffers and target networks help in methods such as DQN. They are methods for specific algorithms. Not all RL needs them.
blocks.548257c7: Further reading: Spinning Up: key concepts and the taxonomy of RL algorithms; Mnih et al. (2015), Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning. The details of algorithms other than the Q-learning example are optional.
blocks.b5852fe4: Training with feedback is different from acting as an agent after deployment. A language model can get RL training and later answer without tools. An agent that uses tools can do a plan–act–observe loop, but it does not change its weights during this interaction. Also, preference optimization includes methods that do not use an online RL algorithm. Keep the training method and the deployed architecture separate. Then you do not think that each LLM agent is an RL learner.
blocks.0dd5fe08: Feedback is also incomplete, and it depends on the social situation. A reward model can show human judgments incorrectly. When we optimize its score, the policy can use these errors. A better match with the preferences does not tell whose preferences are important, or which actions are legitimate. These questions lead to alignment and to the ethics material later in the course.
blocks.5bcadbd2: Until now, we assumed that the transition rules and the reward rules of the environment do not change. When other decision-makers also adapt, the result of an action depends on their decisions and on their learning. Thus, we need a multi-agent view. The delivery robot must negotiate with pedestrians and other robots. It cannot think of them only as fixed obstacles.
blocks.3a536e02: When several agents share an environment, the result for each agent depends on the other agents. The interactions can be cooperative, competitive or mixed. People in traffic coordinate without explicit agreement. Bidders in an auction compete. A team of robots can divide the tasks. From the view of one learner, the environment is non-stationary (it changes over time), because the other agents also change their policies.
blocks.60f0f383: Game theory gives concepts such as best response and equilibrium. Multi-agent RL studies how agents can learn policies through interaction. Communication can help agents to coordinate. But messages can be incomplete, strategic or deceptive. When each agent is capable alone, the system of agents is not automatically effective together. Problems can occur: congestion, free riding (an agent gets the benefit but does not do its part), duplicated work, and chains of incorrect assumptions. Thus, the evaluation must examine the results of the full system: fairness, robustness, use of resources and how failures spread. The score of each agent is not sufficient.
blocks.c37a9564: In a cooperative task, agents share a team reward. But it is still difficult to give credit: the action of which agent caused the success? In a competitive task, when one agent improves, the challenge for the other agents changes. Mixed settings have both. An example is traffic: all drivers want to prevent collisions, but they compete for space and time. Centralized training can use information about all agents. Decentralized execution gives each agent only its local observations.
blocks.f98a8c0d: Communication is an action that has costs and results. Agents must decide what to communicate, to which agent and when. A message can decrease uncertainty, coordinate roles that complete each other, or make common knowledge. But it can also use bandwidth or show the strategy to others. In teams of LLM agents, you can give the roles “researcher”, “critic” and “writer”. This can help the team to cover more of the task. But it can also cause duplicated work. It can also make the same incorrect idea stronger, when all agents use similar models and sources.
blocks.8639c98c: Emergence means that patterns of the full system come from local interactions. Nobody programmed these patterns as a global plan. Flocking can come from simple rules of separation, alignment and cohesion. Congestion can occur when each driver tries to make the travel time as short as possible. Emergence is not automatically intelligent or good. Thus, multi-agent evaluation needs counterfactual tests, groups with different compositions, failures of communication, and measurement of the results of the group, not only the results of each agent.
blocks.a2b54b3f: Craig Reynolds' boids (1987): each boid sees only its neighbours in the view radius. It combines three rules: separation, alignment and cohesion. No rule tells the group to make a flock. Set a rule to 0 to see what that rule adds. Polarization is the length of the average heading vector. It is 1 when all boids fly in the same direction. It is near 0 when their directions are random.
blocks.dbc6f4a5: Reading: Russell and Norvig, 4th ed., Chapter 18. This chapter introduces decision making with many agents, cooperation and competition.
blocks.6cc11091: Robotics brings the ideas above into the physical world. Before the robot can plan or learn a policy, it needs a useful estimate of the state. When a policy selects an action, a controller must still execute it. Thus, we now separate perception, planning and control. We do not think of the agent as one neural network.
blocks.b33feaa8: A robot closes the agent loop in the physical world. Sensors change light, force, sound, distance or joint position into measurements. Actuators make motion. Perception estimates the state that is relevant. Planning selects a route or a sequence of actions. Control changes that plan into motor commands. All of these stages have uncertainty. A wheel slips, something blocks a camera, an object moves, or the environment is different from the training environment.
blocks.c0442507: Six robots get the same perfect commands: drive one side, then turn left by 20°. They do this eighteen times for each lap, so after each lap they must come back to the red start. But each side is a little too long or too short (the wheels slip), and each turn has a small error. Without feedback, a robot knows only the commands that it gave. Thus, each error in the heading turns all the sides after it, and the errors add up, lap after lap. With a position fix (from a landmark, a beacon or a camera), the robot measures where it really is. Then it moves to the corner where it must be. This is the estimate–act–measure–correct loop of the text.
blocks.36bdbf44: Raw sensors do not give a symbolic world that is ready to use. A camera gives arrays of intensity values. Lidar gives distances. An inertial measurement unit gives accelerations and rates of rotation. Perception detects objects, surfaces, people and free space. State estimation combines measurements that have uncertainty over time. For a mobile robot, localization estimates where the robot is, and mapping estimates the environment. Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) does the two tasks together.
blocks.6f079e0f: When you combine sensors, the estimates can become more robust. GPS can drift, or it can stop indoors. Cameras can fail in darkness. Wheel odometry collects more and more error when the wheels slip. Sensor fusion uses the fact that different measurements have different types of errors. The result is still an estimate with uncertainty. It is not the real truth. A planner must behave differently when the localization is precise and when several locations are still possible.
blocks.de7a6d8f: Planning occurs at more than one level. A task planner can decide to get a parcel before it goes to the recipient. A motion planner finds a trajectory through configuration space with no collisions. A local planner reacts to obstacles that are near. A controller continuously changes a wanted trajectory into motor commands and corrects deviations. These layers operate at different timescales. Strategic plans can update every few seconds. Balance control can update hundreds of times each second.
blocks.3eb71842: Classical search is still important here. A* can plan paths on a map. Sampling-based methods, for example rapidly exploring random trees, can work with robot configurations that have many dimensions. Model-predictive control optimizes a short future horizon again and again, and it plans again after new measurements. Learned components can improve perception, predict dynamics or propose actions. But geometric constraints and feedback control still give a useful structure.
blocks.9148b12d: Physical interaction is slow and expensive, and sometimes it is dangerous. Thus, robots often learn or get tests in simulation. But a policy can use details of the simulator that are not true in the real world. Domain randomization changes textures, lighting, friction, mass, delays and sensor noise during training. Thus, the policy cannot depend on the details of one simulated world. If the policy works in many variations, the real world is possibly only one more variation. System identification is a different method: it tries to make the simulator the same as the physical system. Fine-tuning in the real world and careful validation are still necessary.
blocks.1ff6d992: Full autonomy is not always the most useful objective. In shared autonomy, a person gives the intention and the robot helps to do the task. A wheelchair can find which doorway the user wants, and the user keeps the authority. A surgical training system can guide a movement, but the learner still does the action. If the help is too weak, it gives little benefit. If the help is too strong, it can hide errors and stop the development of skills. Thus, the design question is not only “human or robot?”. It is this: how must we divide initiative, information and control over time?
blocks.d0bbce87: Robots also make the risks real and immediate. You can check an incorrect sentence from an LLM before you use it. An incorrect movement of a robot can cause harm immediately. Safe deployment needs redundant sensors, careful operating limits, collision avoidance, emergency stops, tests and a clear division of responsibility. Human supervision must be able to act: if a supervisor cannot understand or stop the system, the supervision has no real meaning.
blocks.d9d80389: Further reading: Dellaert and Hutchinson, Introduction to Robotics and Perception. This book connects the parts of the pipeline: perception, estimation, planning and control. Also see Russell and Norvig, Chapter 26.
blocks.a925f74e: The board, or the history of observations

blocks.3975f139: The same words (environment, observation, action, policy, objective and feedback) connect all three. But their engineering requirements are different, because tools, other agents and physical bodies cause different types of results. When you analyse an agent, ask these questions: What can it observe? What can it change? Which objective does it really optimize? How does it learn or plan? Where can uncertainty come in? Who can intervene? These questions give more information than the question whether the system is “autonomous”.
blocks.d2cb29ed: Agency is a relation between a system and an environment. Reinforcement learning is one method to improve actions from their results. Agentic frameworks connect models to tools and memory. Robotics puts the loop in the physical world, which has uncertainty. The capability depends on the full loop. Safe and intended behaviour depends on objectives, constraints, monitoring and human authority.

blocks.317ae90d: Before we can build an agent, we must describe its job precisely. The classic method of Russell and Norvig is PEAS: Performance measure (what is a good result), Environment (the world where the agent operates), Actuators (how the agent acts on the world) and Sensors (how the agent perceives the world).
blocks.d94e2041: This is a worked example: the PEAS description of a robot vacuum cleaner.
blocks.5adb61b5: How much dirt it cleans, how much energy it uses, how much noise it makes, how much time it needs
blocks.d5e1282e: A room (or a house) with a floor, furniture, dirt and stairs
blocks.472eca28: Wheels (for steering and driving), brushes, vacuum suction
blocks.ee3c520f: When we have PEAS, we can also classify the environment itself in six of the standard dimensions. (We do not use the seventh dimension, known or unknown, from the overview above.)
blocks.b27c185c: Fully or partially observable: can the sensors of the agent see the full state of the environment at each step?
blocks.201ce733: Deterministic or stochastic: does the next state depend only on the current state and the action of the agent? Or is there uncertainty or randomness?
blocks.b674c193: Episodic or sequential: is each pair of percept and action independent of the other pairs? Or do earlier actions have an effect on later actions?
blocks.23aab675: Static or dynamic: can the environment change while the agent thinks about its decision?
blocks.38ec2f17: Discrete or continuous: is there a finite number of different states and actions, or a continuum?
blocks.ab74228e: Single-agent or multi-agent: is our agent alone in the environment? Or are there other agents (cooperative or competitive)?
blocks.1833b52d: The vacuum cleaner above is: partially observable (it cannot see the dirt in the next room); stochastic (bumps and slips occur); sequential (it is important where it cleaned before); dynamic (people walk through and make new dirt); continuous (the robot moves on wheels on the floor; only a simplified model, for example the two-square vacuum world of Russell and Norvig, is discrete); and single-agent (usually).

blocks.21834b7c: We want to tell you some things that we think are important about robotics. First, many robots are already in daily use. Our favourite example is the dishwasher. The first models were invented in approximately 1850. A dishwasher is a robot, because it has sensors that sense its real-world environment (the temperature and the flow of the water, how many dishes there are and how dirty they are, etc.). It also has actuators that let it change its environment (it heats the water, releases the detergent, splashes the water, etc.). With this definition, a radiator thermostat is also a robot, and we agree with that!
blocks.1092c7d4: There is one more thing to know about robotics. It is more difficult to explain in words, and it is the reason why we do not try to go deeper into robotics in this course. In short: it is very difficult to operate in the real world. Sensors are never perfect, and they fail frequently. Thus, it is very difficult to know the state of the system, for example where the robot is in relation to the objects around it. The actuators, for example the motors that move the robot, are also not perfect. When the robot tries to move its hand, or to roll forward on its wheels, by exactly 10 cm, it really moves 9 or 11 cm.
blocks.13ec9d9d: Because of this second problem, robust robotics solutions often need work at a very different level. This level is often “lower” in some sense than in other types of AI applications. Those applications only have to work with simulated environments or static data, not with the real world, which is not clean or predictable.
blocks.c78bea6d: If you can work with real robots, we recommend that you do it. In earlier versions of the course, we did robotics with LEGO Mindstorms robots. But you can program new LEGO hubs, for example the hubs in the SPIKE Prime and MINDSTORMS Robot Inventor sets, in Python, for example with the open-source Pybricks firmware. Raspberry Pi also looks like a good alternative. If you can try one of these, and build and program robots, we think that you will understand what we try to say here!

blocks.240545ec: AI has a larger and larger effect on the real world. Until recently, most AI researchers did not think about these problems. People did not expect them to think about the effects of their work on society. Now, some AI conferences require a broader impact statement or a checklist. The most important example is the NeurIPS conference (see this study). The statement or checklist asks the authors of research articles to think about the effects of their work. blocks.c784a0d9: Look at the case of the US drugstore chain “Rite Aid”. This is a summary in simple words of what the FTC says (FTC US, 2023). Rite Aid used facial recognition technology that is based on artificial intelligence. Its purpose was to identify customers who possibly stole from the shop (shoplifting) or did other problematic things. But the complaint says that the company did not do sufficient things to prevent harm to customers. Thus, employees accused customers of wrong actions, but the customers had done nothing wrong. The reason was that the facial recognition technology incorrectly flagged these customers as a match for a person who was identified earlier as a shoplifter or other troublemaker. The company did not tell the customers that it used the technology in its shops, and it told employees not to give this information. The complaint says that the employees acted on these false positive alerts. They followed customers in the shops, searched them, told them to leave, called the police to confront or remove them, and accused them in public of shoplifting or other wrong actions, sometimes in front of friends or family. Also, the FTC says that the actions of Rite Aid had a larger effect on people of color than on other people.
blocks.2c08f4c5: The Guardian writes this (summary in simple words): Rite Aid had a contract with two private vendors, whose names are not given. Rite Aid made, or told these companies to make, a database of “persons of interest”. The database had images of the persons and other personal information that identifies them. The settlement says that the quality of these images was often low. The images came from the CCTV cameras of Rite Aid, from the facial recognition cameras or from the mobile phones of employees.

blocks.6bee0752: A multi-agent LLM system is a set of model calls that have different roles, instructions or tools. These calls give work to each other. The Anthropic guide Building effective agents (2024) describes the usual patterns, from fixed workflows to open-ended agents:
blocks.0e19e864: Prompt chaining: a fixed sequence of calls. Code does checks between the calls (make an outline, check the outline, write).
blocks.6a651436: Routing: the first call classifies the request. Then it sends the request to a specialized prompt, or to a smaller or larger model.
blocks.bd9c2423: Parallelization: independent parts run at the same time. Or several attempts do the same task, and then they vote.
blocks.ab8d2184: Evaluator–optimizer: one model writes. Another model gives a critique against clear criteria. The loop repeats until the critic approves (see the second listing below).
blocks.ba7aa850: In multi-agent debate (Du et al., ICML 2024), several copies of a model answer the same question. They read the answers of the other copies and change their own answers, for a few rounds. On the benchmarks of the authors, this improved both reasoning and factual accuracy, in comparison with one model.
blocks.9ad5e70e: But more agents also mean more calls, more cost and more possible failures. Cemri et al. (2025) annotated execution traces of popular multi-agent frameworks. They found 14 failure modes in three groups. The first group is errors in the system design (agents ignore their role or the task). The second group is misalignment between agents (they keep information from other agents, ignore the input of other agents or move away from the task). The third group is weak verification (they stop too early or check nothing). Also, the text above tells you that agents that use the same model have the same blind spots. A good rule is this: start with one agent and good tools. Add agents only when a measurement shows that they help.
blocks.cdd80335: The memory for the weights of a model is approximately the number of parameters, multiplied by the bits for each weight, divided by eight. An example: a model with 8 billion parameters needs approximately 16 GB at 16 bits. At the 4-bit quantization that Ollama uses by default, it needs only approximately 5 GB. Long conversations also need the KV cache (see the bonus of Week 5). For a model with the shape of Llama 3 8B, this is 128 KiB for each token, thus 1 GiB for 8192 tokens. If all of this fits in the memory of a GPU, or in the unified memory of a Mac with Apple silicon, the model answers quickly. If it does not fit, the model runs on the CPU, more slowly.
blocks.2ed466d0: The Ollama server that you installed in Week 5 also gives an API at http://localhost:11434. It has an endpoint under /v1 that is compatible with OpenAI. The llama-server of llama.cpp and LM Studio give the same type of endpoint. Code that uses this interface works in the same way when the model runs on your laptop or in the cloud. For agents, select a model that was trained for tool calling (the model library of Ollama marks these models with the tag tools), for example ollama pull qwen3:8b (approximately 5 GB). Small models with 1 to 4 billion parameters can call simple tools, but they make more mistakes in tasks with many steps. blocks.3f7a9b91: The writer and the critic are the same model with different instructions. Thus, they have the same blind spots. A stronger setup gives the critic a different model. Or, where it is possible, it replaces the critic with a check in code, for example a run of tests.
blocks.91aa5449: Keep the model server local. By default, Ollama listens only on 127.0.0.1:11434, and it has no authentication: each person who can get to the port can use your models. Do not set OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0, and do not forward the port on a network that you do not control.
blocks.1bc12f8f: Least privilege. Give each tool the smallest power that works: read-only before write, one folder and not the full disk, no shell. Run agents that execute code in a container or a virtual machine. It must have no network access and only a copy of the files that the agent needs.
blocks.e53b1af0: Do not trust anything that the agent reads. Web pages, e-mails, documents and tool results can contain instructions (prompt injection). Simon Willison uses the name lethal trifecta for the combination of three things: access to private data, contact with content that is not trusted, and a method to communicate outside. An attacker can trick an agent that has all three, so that it sends your data to the attacker. Remove a minimum of one of the three.
blocks.0701a76a: Humans approve important actions. Before the agent sends, deletes, pays or publishes, it must wait for your confirmation. Budgets for steps, time and tokens stop loops that do not end. A log of each tool call shows what occurred.
blocks.79d10480: Keep secrets where the agent cannot get them. Put API keys in environment variables. Never put them in prompts or in files that the agent can read. Give agents their own accounts with limited rights.
blocks.6ae10105: Be careful with the supply chain. Download models, agent plugins and MCP servers only from sources that you trust. Use the safetensors and GGUF formats when possible. They were designed to keep weights without executable code. Do not use checkpoints that are based on pickle (.pt, .bin) when possible, because they can run any code when you load them. An MCP server is a program that runs with your permissions.
